levels: AI is in use, but the rules and owners are not yet in place. A few early steps will remove most of the exposure.
Some foundations exist. Closing the gaps below will turn good intentions into a framework you can evidence.
Your governance is in good shape. Tightening the weaker areas will prepare you for external scrutiny.
You govern AI to a high standard. Formal assurance, such as ISO/IEC 42001 certification, is a natural next step.

questions.title: What sensitive data could reach AI tools in your organisation?

options.label: Personal data of clients, customers or citizens

questions.title: Is a named person or committee accountable for how AI is used?
rec: Name an accountable owner
Give one senior person or a small committee clear responsibility for AI use, with authority to approve, pause or stop it.

options.label: It falls to IT or whoever is interested
Yes, a named owner with a written mandate

questions.title: Do you have a written policy on acceptable AI use?
rec: Publish an acceptable AI use policy
Set out approved tools, data limits and review rules in plain language, and make sure every member of staff has read it.

options.label: A draft or general IT policy only
Yes, but it is not widely known

questions.title: Do you keep a register of the AI tools in use?
rec: Build an AI register
List every AI tool in use, who uses it, what data it touches and its risk level. Most organisations find tools they did not know about.

options.label: We know some of the tools
A complete register, kept up to date

questions.title: Must new AI tools be approved before staff use them?
rec: Create an approval route
Agree a short, fast process for approving new AI tools, so staff have a safe way to say yes.

options.label: Yes, every tool goes through a set route

questions.title: Do staff have clear rules on what data may go into AI tools?
rec: Set clear data rules
Tell staff which categories of data must never enter a public AI tool, and give them an approved option for sensitive work.

options.label: Clear rules for everyone, with examples

questions.title: How do you handle staff using personal AI accounts for work?
rec: Move work onto approved accounts
Provide organisation-managed AI accounts with the right data settings and ask staff to stop using personal ones for work.

options.label: Discouraged, with approved options for some

questions.title: Are AI-assisted outputs checked before they reach clients, students or decisions?
rec: Check outputs before they leave
Require a named reviewer for AI-assisted work that goes to clients, students or decision makers, and record that the check took place.

questions.title: Do you assess risk before using AI in high-impact areas such as hiring, grading, credit or eligibility?
rec: Assess high-impact uses first
Run an impact assessment before AI touches decisions about people, covering fairness, accuracy, data protection and appeal routes.

questions.title: Have staff been trained on responsible AI use?
rec: Train your people
Give staff practical training on safe AI use and give leaders a briefing on accountability, then record who has completed it.

options.label: All relevant staff trained and recorded

questions.title: Can staff report AI errors or incidents, and is there a plan to respond?
rec: Set up incident reporting
Give staff a simple way to report AI errors or data leaks, and agree who investigates and how fast.

options.label: A route exists but no plan
Yes, a route and a tested response plan

notes.ng: Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 applies to personal data entered into AI tools, including tools hosted abroad.
notes.uk: UK GDPR and ICO guidance on AI apply to any personal data your AI tools process.
notes.eu: The EU AI Act places duties on organisations that deploy AI, alongside GDPR.
notes.multi: Operating across borders means several regimes apply at once. Map AI use against each one, starting with the strictest.
notes.personal: Personal data is in scope, so data protection impact assessments should cover your AI tools.
notes.records: Student or patient records carry a higher duty of care and should only reach approved, contracted AI tools.
notes.fin: Financial information calls for strong access controls and clear retention rules in any AI tool.
notes.conf: Confidential documents should only reach AI tools that contractually exclude training on your data.
